title: Where could a data center be built in Norfolk, what rules would it follow, and who decides?
summary: As of November 19, 2026: Norfolk's Zoning Ordinance has no data center use; City staff say data centers have been treated as offices, and the Office use covers data processing facilities. Staff count two data centers in the city, both tenants in office buildings, with no negative impacts noted; Virginia Business reported on September 29, 2026 that Norfolk had had no serious inquiries from developers. After a staff briefing on August 13, the Planning Commission on October 22, 2026 recommended 4 to 0 (three absent) a text amendment creating two uses: small-scale data centers (standalone, under 30,000 square feet and under 25 megawatts), allowed by right in the O, BC-O, BC-I, I-L, I-G and IN-C districts, and large-scale ones, allowed only with a Conditional Use Permit in I-G, I-DW, BC-I and BC-O. Every data center would file an impact assessment (sound on homes and schools within 500 feet, water, parks, historic sites, forestland) under Code of Virginia §15.2-2209.5, whose own requirement starts at 100 megawatts and leaves local zoning authority intact; under Exhibit D noise would be held to City Code Chapter 26 with exceptions, and equipment screened. The transmittal letter, staff report and Proposed Text also require a hazardous materials discharge plan, but Exhibit D, the ordinance's text of the standards, doesn't. City Council decides; as of November 19 no Council hearing date was found (the December 1 and 15 agendas weren't posted).

findings.claim: Under the Zoning Ordinance in force today, the Office use's definition includes data processing facilities among the business functions it covers; the ordinance names no data center use.

what_would_help.text: Before Council votes, residents can speak at the Council meeting where it is heard or write to Council. The Council Transmittal Letter lists no proponents or opponents at the Planning Commission hearing.
Ask whether the hazardous materials discharge plan described in the transmittal letter and staff report is meant to be in the adopted text: Exhibit D, attached to the ordinance, leaves it out.

If the amendment passes, a large-scale data center would go through a Conditional Use Permit, with a Planning Commission hearing and a Council vote (see case file norfolk-zoning-use-tables-cup for how a permit is judged). A small-scale one would not; its impact assessment goes to the Zoning Administrator.

records_to_request: The staff presentation on data centers given to the Planning Commission on August 13, 2026, and any minutes of that item (Department of City Planning).

The final ordinance text to go to City Council on the data center amendment, and an explanation of whether the hazardous materials discharge plan is included (City Attorney / Department of City Planning).
Any inquiries, pre-application meetings or correspondence with data center developers about Norfolk sites since January 1, 2025 (Department of Economic Development; Department of City Planning).

Records identifying the zoning classification and floor area of the two existing data centers staff referred to, and any power-demand information the City holds for them (Department of City Planning).
pending: When City Council will hear and vote on the amendment: the Planning Commission recommended it on October 22, 2026; as of November 19 the Council agendas for December 1 and 15 weren't posted, and no Council date was found in the legislative record.

Which text Council is asked to adopt: Exhibit D leaves out the hazardous materials discharge plan that the transmittal letter, staff report and Proposed Text include; adds a construction-or-demolition noise exception the letter doesn't list; applies Chapter 26 with exceptions to small-scale centers where the letter says no perceptible noise from mechanical systems except testing and emergencies (and its own small-scale definition says none at any time); and drops 'prior to zoning approval' and 'with mitigation measures as necessary' from the assessment.

Which districts appear in the use-table exhibits (A, B, C): the rows read 'Data Center, Small Scale' with P and 'Data Center, Large Scale' with C, but a table column can't be quoted exactly, so the districts are taken from the transmittal letter and staff report.
How much land in the named districts could hold a large-scale data center: not measured yet (the I-G, I-DW, BC-I and BC-O parcels could be counted from the City's zoning layer).

Whether a data center inside an office building that isn't standalone would still be an Office use under the amendment: the small-scale definition says standalone, and the record read so far doesn't say.
